10.1002_adfm.79134: Nonradiative recombination in perovskite solar cells (PSCs) is fundamentally governed by carrier‐defect interactions, yet existing strategies primarily focus on defect density reduction and interfacial passivation. Here, we establish a guanidinium‐based dielectric strategy to regulate carrier‐defect interaction kinetics in perovskite films. By incorporating guanidinium‐based additives with systematically varied molecular dipole moments and polarizabilities, enhanced dielectric screening is achieved, which weakens carrier‐defect interactions while simultaneously reducing nonradiative loss. Together with multifunctional chemical passivation, this leads to suppressed nonradiative recombination and reduced energy dissipation. As a result, the optimized devices achieve efficiencies of 26.15% and 26.39% for n‐i‐p and p‐i‐n architectures, respectively, along with 25.64% for large area (1 cm 2 ) devices and 23.11% for wide‐bandgap (1.68 eV) PSCs. The devices also exhibit excellent operational, thermal, and ambient stability. This work identifies dielectric regulation of carrier‐defect interactions as a general strategy to minimize energy dissipation and advance PSCs toward their radiative efficiency limits.
10.1002_adma.202511444: Achieving efficient ion transport in thick electrodes remains a fundamental challenge in electrochemical systems with high energy density, primarily due to prolonged diffusion pathways and poorly integrated architectures. Leveraging the nanoconfinement effect, (sub)nanoscale channels can significantly accelerate ion transport kinetics to maximize electrochemical performance. Inspired by the hierarchical network structure of bamboo membrane, a gradient nanoconfined MXene electrode (GNC‐MX) is designed, where multiscale interlayer spacing is coupled with in‐plane mesopores that bridge adjacent nanoconfined channels, enabling synergistic vertical and horizontal ion migration. Finite element simulations and density functional theory calculations reveal the synergistic optimization mechanism of ion transport via the gradient nanoconfined channels and in‐plane mesopores. Compared to pristine MXene, GNC‐MX electrodes exhibit substantially enhanced ion transport kinetics and charge storage performance. To optimize the nanoconfined channels, an in situ deprotonation‐reprotonation strategy is introduced to strengthen electrostatic repulsion and weaken hydrogen bonding and van der Waals interactions of the MXene interlayer, enabling quasi‐permanent expansion of ion transport channels. Furthermore, a scalable group‐welding method is developed to fabricate 400 µm‐thick electrodes with an ultrahigh areal capacitance of 20.7 F cm −2 , surpassing current MXene‐based electrodes. This work provides a scalable and tunable biomimetic platform for advanced ion nanoconfinement in energy storage systems.
10.1002_aenm.70950: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are promising candidates for next‐generation photovoltaics thanks to their high power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) and cost‐effective fabrication processes. However, reliance on noble metal electrodes, such as gold (Au) and silver (Ag), significantly increases overall device cost. This work demonstrates high‐performance PSCs with noble‐metal‐free multilayer electrodes comprising molybdenum oxide (MoO X ), chromium (Cr), and aluminum (Al). These PSCs achieve a PCE of 25.6%, which is competitive with that of Au‐based devices (26.3%). Furthermore, a mini‐module with an aperture area of 25.5 cm 2 shows a PCE of 21.3%, which indicates the scalability of the proposed electrode architecture to large‐area devices. Systematic investigation of each layer shows that the MoO X layer functions as an effective diffusion barrier that suppresses metal‐ion migration. The intermediate Cr layer enhances interfacial adhesion and reduces series resistance. In addition, the MoO X /Cr/Al multilayer electrode exhibits significantly higher resistance to external scratching than Au electrodes, which demonstrates improved mechanical durability. These results show that MoO X /Cr/Al multilayer electrodes provide a practical alternative to noble metals and substantially enhance the cost competitiveness of PSCs.
10.1021_acs.analchem.5c07453: Optical spectroscopy of functional dyes is the most used tool for organic, organometallic, and inorganic chromophores. This technical note discusses the coupling of magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) spectroscopy with a conventional spectroelectrochemical (SE) cell setup. The discussed approach allows for the study of in situ ligand and metal centered reduction and oxidation processes. Advantages and limitations of the proposed method will be discussed on the basis of transition-metal phthalocyanines and chlorophyll A chromophores. Reported methods can be used not only for SE-MCD experiments with organic chromophores but also to study redox processes in inorganic and organometallic complexes.
10.1021_acsami.6c10920: Solid-state sodium metal batteries are promising candidates for grid-scale energy storage due to their inherent safety and low cost. However, the development of solid electrolytes that support high-rate (>20 C) cycling for fast-charging applications remains a major challenge. Herein, we explore how adding SiO2 affects the ionic conductivity and dendrite suppression of NaB3H8, to develop superior solid electrolytes for high-rate batteries. The composites featuring an amorphous passivating layer with B-O bonds were fabricated via ball milling. Among them, NaB3H8-40%SiO2 exhibits the best conductivity, reaching 0.62 mS cm-1 at 25 °C, 2 orders of magnitude higher than that of pristine NaB3H8. Crucially, by reducing electronic conductivity and enhancing mechanical strength, it possesses a high critical current density of up to 6.5 mA cm-2, significantly higher than that of other reported hydridoborates. The Na/NaB3H8-40%SiO2/TiS2 batteries exhibit superior rate capability (216.4 mAh g-1 at 1 C and 143.1 mAh g-1 at 20 C) and long-term cycling stability (nearly 100.0% capacity retention after 2000 cycles at 20 C) at 30 °C. This work offers a promising approach for the development of innovative solid electrolytes in fast-charging or high-power-density sodium metal batteries.
